what-is-agentic-analytics.title: What is agentic analytics
what-is-agentic-analytics.why: Analytics leaders judge this architecture by one outcome: an agent that answers business questions from governed data and shows where each number came from.

the-stack.title: The agentic stack
the-stack.why: When an agent gives a wrong answer, leaders need to know which layer failed: the model, the harness, or the interfaces and data underneath. That decides what to fix and what to buy.

from-dashboards-to-questions.title: From dashboards to questions
from-dashboards-to-questions.why: Dashboards answer the questions someone planned for. Agents take the ones nobody planned for, which changes what the business should expect from its BI spend.

why-the-lakehouse.title: Why an open lakehouse
why-the-lakehouse.why: Agents multiply the number of readers and questions. The business case for an open lakehouse is that one governed copy of the data can serve all of them.

semantic-layer-as-contract.title: The semantic layer as an agent contract
semantic-layer-as-contract.why: The semantic layer is where the business writes down what revenue, churn, and active customer mean. Without it, an agent's fluent guess becomes a wrong number in a meeting.

text-to-sql-and-its-limits.title: Text to SQL and why it stalls
text-to-sql-and-its-limits.why: Generating SQL is easy. Generating the SQL the business agrees is correct is not, and that gap decides whether a pilot earns trust.

governance-for-agents.title: Governance for agents
governance-for-agents.why: An agent must not reach data its user cannot, and you must be able to prove it afterwards. That is the first question risk and audit teams will ask.

evaluation-and-trust.title: Evaluation and trust
evaluation-and-trust.why: Leaders do not adopt agents because of benchmark scores. They adopt them when answers can be checked, traced, and reproduced.

cost-and-latency.title: Cost and latency
cost-and-latency.why: Agents replace a few large queries with many small ones, which changes where the analytics budget goes and what is worth optimizing.

portability-and-lock-in.title: Portability and lock-in
portability-and-lock-in.why: Every component choice carries a replacement cost later. Leaders should know which parts of the stack are hardest to swap before they sign.

enterprise-rollout.title: Rolling this out enterprise wide
enterprise-rollout.why: A pilot that impresses a steering committee is not yet a capability the whole company uses. The order of the rollout matters as much as the architecture.

the-harness.title: The harness
the-harness.why: Most agent behavior comes from the harness: context, tools, retries, and when to stop. That is where reliability is won or lost.

one-copy-many-readers.title: One copy, many readers
one-copy-many-readers.why: Copies of data produce agents that disagree with each other. One governed copy keeps answers consistent across teams.

the-model.title: The model
the-model.why: Model choice gets the attention, but it is one layer of three. Treating it as the whole architecture leads to the wrong purchase.

open-interfaces.title: Open interfaces
open-interfaces.why: The interfaces an agent speaks through should be specifications, not products. A closed one makes every later tool change expensive.

/what-is-agentic-lakehouse/.title: What is an agentic lakehouse?
/what-is-agentic-lakehouse/.how: The engineering side is the agentic lakehouse: open Iceberg tables, a semantic layer, governance enforced at query time, and an agent interface such as an MCP server.

/agentic-lakehouse-architecture/.title: Agentic lakehouse architecture
/agentic-lakehouse-architecture/.how: Engineers build this as a layered reference architecture: object storage, Iceberg tables, a catalog, a query engine, a semantic layer, and an MCP agent interface, with governance across the middle.

/agentic-bi/.title: Agentic BI
/agentic-bi/.how: Engineers build agentic BI by giving agents federated, governed access to data where it already lives.

/kb/autonomous-data-agents/.title: Autonomous data agents
/kb/autonomous-data-agents/.how: Engineers put a model to work on data as an autonomous data agent with tools, scoped credentials, and a stopping rule.

/kb/safe-action-loops/.title: Safe action loops
/kb/safe-action-loops/.how: Engineers build the harness as a safe action loop: plan, query, check the result, and stop inside explicit limits.

/kb/llm-data-access/.title: LLM data access
/kb/llm-data-access/.how: Engineers expose data to models through defined, governed access paths instead of raw database credentials.

/kb/agentic-lakehouse/.title: Agentic lakehouse
/kb/agentic-lakehouse/.how: Engineers build the substrate as an agentic lakehouse on open table formats, with a semantic layer and governed query execution on top.

/kb/multi-engine-data-architecture/.title: Multi-engine data architecture
/kb/multi-engine-data-architecture/.how: Engineers keep one copy by letting several engines read the same Iceberg tables through a shared catalog.

/kb/ai-semantic-layer/.title: AI semantic layer
/kb/ai-semantic-layer/.how: Engineers implement the contract as an AI semantic layer that maps raw schemas to governed business definitions agents can query.

/kb/ai-agent-authorization/.title: AI agent authorization
/kb/ai-agent-authorization/.how: Engineers enforce this with agent authorization patterns that carry the user's identity and permissions into every query an agent runs.

/kb/trustworthy-ai-execution/.title: Trustworthy AI execution
/kb/trustworthy-ai-execution/.how: Engineers make agent answers checkable and reproducible at the execution layer, where every query can be logged and replayed.

/kb/lakehouse-cost-optimization/.title: Lakehouse cost optimization
/kb/lakehouse-cost-optimization/.how: Engineers control the cost of many small agent queries with caching, pruning, and acceleration in the lakehouse.

/kb/enterprise-ai-agents/.title: Enterprise AI agents
/kb/enterprise-ai-agents/.how: Engineers take agents from pilot to production with shared identity, governance, and semantic definitions.

/kb/lakehouse-interoperability/.title: Lakehouse interoperability
/kb/lakehouse-interoperability/.how: Engineers keep components swappable by building on open table formats, open catalogs, and open protocols.

/kb/text-to-sql/.title: Text-to-SQL
/kb/text-to-sql/.how: Engineers close the text-to-SQL gap by grounding generation in a semantic layer instead of raw schemas.

/kb/semantic-layer/.title: Semantic layer
/kb/semantic-layer/.how: Engineers implement shared definitions as a semantic layer that agents and BI tools query through.

/patterns/agent-safe-governed-views/.title: Agent-safe governed views
/patterns/agent-safe-governed-views/.how: Engineers give agents governed views instead of raw tables: curated columns, joins written once, and an engine that cannot read anything else.

/patterns/row-and-column-policies-for-ag.title: Row and column policies for agents
/patterns/row-and-column-policies-for-ag.how: Engineers tie what an agent sees to the identity it acts for, with row filters baked into governed views and restricted metrics refused by name.

/patterns/query-guardrails-for-agents/.title: Query guardrails for agents
/patterns/query-guardrails-for-agents/.how: Engineers cap agent queries with allowlists, row limits, timeouts, and cost caps estimated from Iceberg metadata before anything runs.

/patterns/semantic-layer-over-mcp/.title: Exposing a semantic layer to agents over MCP
/patterns/semantic-layer-over-mcp/.how: Engineers expose metrics and dimensions as MCP tools, so the agent picks a business definition and the server writes the SQL.

/patterns/mcp-server-over-iceberg-catalo.title: An MCP server over an Iceberg catalog
/patterns/mcp-server-over-iceberg-catalo.how: Engineers build the agent interface on an Iceberg catalog, using table metadata to scope and cost each request.

/patterns/.title: Implementation patterns
/patterns/.how: Engineers make answers checkable by returning the SQL behind every number and logging every agent query, allowed or refused.
